newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Low tax revenue could hit reform - Russian minister.
newsitem.headline: Low tax revenue could hit reform - Russian minister.

text.p: Low levels of tax collection could threaten the course of economic reform in Russia and force the government to borrow heavily on financial markets, Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said on Thursday.
Tax revenues in the first nine months of this year amounted to 138 trillion roubles or 74 percent of targeted volume, the government said in a statement.
Unless tax collection improved, the government would have to consider changing its current economic course, Interfax news agency quoted Livshits as saying.
"Never before have we been so close to the point, where we either collect revenues or we shall have to think how to change the course," Livshits told a cabinet meeting, according to Interfax.

This would mean a turn to heavy borrowing on domestic financial markets, just as the finance ministry is trying to curb borrowing costs by issuing only enough government securities to repay maturing issues, Livshits said.
The Russian economy is mired in a payments crisis in which firms do not pay suppliers or workers and huge tax arrears are built up.
Last week President Boris Yeltsin set up an emergency commission headed by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to improve tax revenues.
Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov submitted a draft resolution to the government on Thursday to cut gas, electricity and railway transport charges.
The aim would be to make it easier for customers to pay their bills and increase tax revenues, he told a news conference.
The government statement said there was a net tax shortfall of 53.6 trillion roubles.
Rodionov suggested cutting gas prices by 15 percent, electricity prices by 20 percent and railway transportation prices by up to 20 percent.

"It will not, of course, solve all problems, but this is the first necessary step to change the trend in the national economy," he said, adding that the economy and finance ministries opposed the draft plan.
Rodionov said firms in the oil and gas sector were the biggest debtor, with tax arrears of 10 trillion roubles.
This week the government threatened six big companies with bankruptcy, if they fail to pay tax arrears within a week.
Officials of some of the companies said on Thursday they had settled their bills not in cash but in kind.
Worry over low tax revenue led the International Monetary Fund to delay payment of a tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia earlier this year.
An IMF mission is currently in Moscow, discussing the release of a new tranche. Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said on Wednesday that the talks would be difficult.
The IMF insists that Russia adhere to economic performance targets, including the budget deficit.
Livshits said he opposed increasing the deficit, which would mean a change in economic policy.
